**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Regle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections » (3 sections : A 1800-1922, B 1922-1961, C 1961 to present, 4 questions chacune, numerotation continue 1 a 12). `regles_choix` porte le minimum impose, une regle `parmi 1 sur 4` par section ; la regle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiee dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question est imprimee « (25 marks) » et la page de garde dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` de l'exercice et de la question unique valent 25. Aucun ecart avec le sujet (4 x 25 = 100).

Defauts d'impression du sujet : scan de deux pages (CamScanner) avec filigrane gcerevision.com et bandeau publicitaire, sans incidence sur la lecture, mais avec une legere transparence de texte (verso) en haut de la page 2 et entre quelques questions ; les intitules de section sont imprimes avec un tiret demi-cadratin (« 1800 - 1922 ») recopie avec un tiret simple ; la question 2 est imprimee « succeed to extend » (tournure incorrecte, recopiee telle quelle) ; la question 3 est ambigue (« the results of German annexation by 1884 ») ; la question 6 est maladroite (« indigenous resistance and failure against French rule »). Aucune figure, carte ni document dans le sujet. Page de garde verifiee : ADVANCED LEVEL, History 2, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, JUNE 2026 (reference GCE26/0760/2/BN).

Aucun corrige officiel : les corriges sont des reponses modeles redigees de memoire, sans acces a une source. Les dates, noms et traites sont ceux de l'historiographie etablie ; les faits dont la precision est moindre sont formules prudemment ou sans chiffre. Aucune citation, statistique ni source n'est inventee. Les corriges sont a relire par un historien du Cameroun avant diffusion.

Question 2 : l'enonce imprime « succeed to extend » (tournure incorrecte pour « succeed in extending »), recopie tel quel. Les dates du jihad (1804, drapeau remis a Modibbo Adama vers 1806, fondation de Yola en 1841, mort d'Adama en 1848) sont celles de l'historiographie courante ; les noms des fondateurs des lamidats (Ngaoundere, Tibati, Banyo, Tignere, Rey-Bouba, Garoua) ne sont volontairement pas donnes, ni les dates de leur fondation.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Under what circumstances and for what reasons did the Fulani succeed to extend their authority in North Cameroon in the 19th century?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** North Cameroon (the Adamawa plateau, the Benue basin and the plains toward Lake Chad) was settled before 1800 by many small, mostly non-Muslim societies (Mbum, Gbaya, Vute, Dii, Fali, Matakam, Mofu, Kapsiki and others, often called "Kirdi"), alongside older states such as Mandara and Bornu in the far north. In the early 19th century the Fulani (Fulbe), who had long lived as herders in this region and elsewhere in the savanna, established their authority over most of the Adamawa plateau and the Benue valley. Their success must be explained by the circumstances in which it took place and by the strengths of the Fulani and the weaknesses of their opponents.

**1. The circumstances.**
(a) *The jihad of Usman dan Fodio.* In 1804, in Hausaland (present northern Nigeria), the Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio launched a jihad against Hausa rulers accused of corrupt government and impure Islam, and founded the Sokoto Caliphate. The movement spread among Fulani communities across the savanna.
(b) *The Adamawa jihad.* Modibbo Adama, a Fulani scholar from the Gurin area, received a flag from Usman dan Fodio (about 1806) and was charged with leading the holy war in "Fombina", the southern lands, which included northern Cameroon. He founded the emirate of Adamawa (his capital was moved to Yola in 1841) under the authority of Sokoto. His lieutenants, the *lamibe* (singular *lamido*), founded or took over centres such as Ngaoundere, Tibati, Banyo, Tignere, Rey-Bouba and Garoua and ruled them as semi-autonomous lamidates.
(c) *Earlier Fulani settlement.* Fulani groups were already living in the region as cattle-keepers and traders, and their communities supplied the first followers and a base for the conquest.

**2. The reasons for their success.**
(a) *Religious unity and legitimacy.* The jihad gave the Fulani a common cause, a sense of mission and a legitimate reason to fight "unbelievers". Islam also gave them literate scholars (*mallams*), a legal code and a system of administration, which made it possible to organise and to hold conquered land.
(b) *Military superiority.* The Fulani fought as mounted warriors, with cavalry, discipline and mobility, against peoples who mostly fought on foot with spears, bows and shields. The savanna and plateau were good horse country, which favoured them.
(c) *Political weakness of the opponents.* Most societies of the plateau and of the hills were small, fragmented chiefdoms or village communities with no standing army and no habit of acting together. The Fulani defeated them one by one, or won them over with alliances and promises of protection, and some local rulers accepted vassalage rather than fight.
(d) *Support from Sokoto.* The backing of the Caliphate gave the leaders prestige, ideas of government and the right to appoint rulers and to receive reinforcements of fighters and scholars.
(e) *Economic motives and resources.* Conquest brought slaves, tribute and cattle. Captives worked on estates and in households or were sent as tribute and sold, which financed more fighting; trade with Hausaland and Bornu brought horses, cloth and other goods. Grazing land for large herds was another aim.
(f) *Leadership and administration.* Capable leaders such as Modibbo Adama and the lamibe organised conquered areas into lamidates with a hierarchy of officials, taxes (including a cattle tax) and courts, which gave their rule stability.
(g) *Assimilation and intermarriage.* Marriages with local families, the conversion of some leaders and the integration of local people into the lamidates reduced opposition over time.

**3. Limits.** Fulani authority was far from total. In the forest and the tsetse fly belt the cavalry and the herds could not advance, so the advance toward the south was checked. Some hill peoples kept their independence by withdrawing to their mountains, and the older states of Mandara and Bornu were not conquered. Well-organised chiefdoms of the Grassfields, such as Bamum, were not overrun either. The lamidates were also far from Sokoto, and their loyalty to it weakened over time. At the end of the century the German conquest (1899-1902), led by officers such as Hans Dominik, ended the independence of the lamidates, though the Germans, and later the British and French, kept the Fulani chiefs as intermediaries.

**Conclusion.** The Fulani extended their authority in North Cameroon because the jihad of Usman dan Fodio and the leadership of Modibbo Adama gave them a unifying religious cause and a strong organisation, because they had cavalry and the support of Sokoto, and because their opponents were divided and militarily weak. Their expansion stopped where nature (the tsetse fly and the forest) or well-organised states resisted.
